info.title: Linking Siliko Core with Your Project

article.para: Siliko Core itself uses CMake for its own build process, however CMake is not required to build or deploy a program that uses Siliko Core. Programs using Siliko Core can be built using a variety of methods.

section.title: General Information
section.para: Your final Siliko Core installation should take one of two forms. On most systems, it will take a typical package layout, and on macOS it will default to being built as a macOS framework, but this can be changed when you build Siliko Core. See Building Siliko Core for more information on building Siliko Core itself, how to select between the typical layout, and the framework on macOS, and where the various files go in each layout.

section.title: The API Header File
section.para: When you build Siliko itself, CMake will generate a header file called Api.h. This is installed with other header files at <SilikoCore/Api.h>. This file is referenced from the other headers with an #include statement. It contains #define statements for exposing public APIs in Siiko Core. Because of platform-specific quirks, it is generated specific to the compiler you use, and whether Siliko Core was built as a shared library (DLL on Windows), or as a static library.

This file is constructed such that nothing special is needed to use the specific build of Siliko Core with which it was generated. If you need to install both a static build and a shared build of Siliko Core to the same location, you should install the version of Api.h that was generated with the shared build of Siiko Core. If you do so, you will have to pass SILIKOCORE_STATIC_DEFINE as a preprocessor #define when building a program that links with the static library. The SILIKOCORE_STATIC_DEFINE define is safe to use with an Api.h file generated for a shared build or a static build. (It is essentially a no-op when using the Api.h from a static build.) So, if you need to automate a build using a static version of Siliko Core, it’s a good idea to define SILIKOCORE_STATIC_DEFINE indiscriminently. If you wish to build using a shared/DLL copy of Siliko Core, you will need the Api.h file that was generated with the shared library you are using.

section.title: Building Using CMake
section.para: As part of building Siliko Core, CMake generates Config package files to use Siliko Core in another CMake project. To use these in your own build process, you will need to do three things. The firstthing is that you will need to find the SilikoCore package with the find_package CMake command.
This will add a Siliko::SilikoCore target to your project. The second thing that you need to do is to link your own target with the Siliko::SilikoCore target using target_link_libraries:
section.programlisting: add_executable(MyProgram) target_sources(MyProgram PRIVATE myprog.c) target_link_libraries(MyProgram PRIVATE Siliko::SilikoCore)
section.para: Finally, you will need to put Siliko in a location where CMake can find it. A full treatment of where CMake looks for dependencies is found in CMake’s documentation.

As part of the build process for Siliko Core, you should have installed it using cmake --install. section.title: Building with GCC and Clang
section.para:
Building a program that uses Siliko Core can be done manually with GCC and Clang. To do this, you will need to pass two options, one when compiling any source files that #include a header provided by Siliko Core, and you will need to add the Siliko Core library when linking. Assuming you have a Unix-style layout for your installation into $HOME/stage/siliko-core you would compile your source file like so:
$CC -I$HOME/stage/siliko-core/include main.c
Where the $CC command could be substituted with gcc or clang, whichever one you are using.
Then, when linking your program, link with the library as such:

Notice that main.o comes before -lSilikoCore on the command line. If you are linking with a static build of SilikoCore, you will need to put any object files, like main.o, that use functions or data provided by SilikoCore before -lSilikoCore on the command line to link due to the way GNU ld and lld scan for functions and data in static libraries when linking.

section.title: A Special Note for GCC and Clang on Windows
section.para: Dynamic link libraries on Windows are built with two components: the DLL file itself, used by the program at runtime, and an import library used at built time to embed information about the DLL into the program. With GCC and Clang Import libraries are given the same name as the DLL, followed by .a. So, a DLL called SilikoCore.dll will have a companion import library called SilikoCore.dll.a. Use the SilikoCore.dll.a file when building your program, and deploy the SilikoCore.dll file with your application.

section.title: Building with Microsoft Visual C++ (Command Line)
section.para: Make sure your shell environment is setup to build. The easiest way to do this is to use the Developer Powershell or Developer Command Prompt items int he Start menu under the submenu for Visual Studio. For full details on setting this up, see Use the Microsoft C++ toolset from the command line in Microsoft’s documentation.

When compiling with Siliko Core, you will need to pass the path to Siliko Core’s header files to cl. You can use a simple /I option to pass the header files’ location, or, if you wish to disable diagnostic messages for the headers, you can use /external:I to specify the header files’ location, and /external:W0 to disable warnings for the headers.

If you built Siliko Core as a shared library (DLL), you will need to include SilikoCore.dll with your executable.

section.title: Building with Xcode
section.para: When building your own program with Xcode, it is best to build Siliko Core as a framework. Then add it as a framework to your project. To do this, first build Siliko Core and install it to a staging directory such as $HOME/stage/siliko.

Open your project in Xcode, and, in the project navigator, select your app. In the Build Settings tab, find Framework Search Paths. In a default installation, it can be found by selecting All, and navigating to the Search Paths section. Add the directory holding SilikoCore.framework to the Framework Search Paths value. In this example, that would be $HOME/stage/siliko/Frameworks. Finally, in the General tab find Frameworks, Libraries, and Embedded Content. Click the + button, and in the windows that opens, select Add Other..., then Add files.... Find and select the Siliko.Framework directory, and click the Open button.

section.title: Building with Visual Studio
section.para: To use Siliko Core within Visual Studio, you will need to add three configuration options to your project settings. These options are all set in the project settings dialog, which you can access under the Project menu, with the [Your Project] Properties item. These instructions assume that you have built and installed Siliko Core to a staging directory, such as %USERPROFILE%\stage\siliko.

To enable compiling your project and allow IntelliSense to find Siliko Core’s types, names and other symbols, you will need to add the include subdirectory to the Additional Include Directories value under C/C++ → General.

To enable linking with the Siliko Core library when building your program, you will need to add the lib subdirectory to the Additional Library Directories value under Linker → General, and add SilikoCore.lib to the Additional Dependencies value under Linker → Input.

And finally, to allow the debugger to find Siliko Core when testing and running your program if you built Siliko Core as a shared library, you will need to add the bin directory where SilikoCore.dll is located to the %PATH% environment variable. You can set this under Debugging by adding a line, such as PATH=%USERPROFILE%\stage\siliko\bin to the Environment value.
